governanceNotes: Duplicate-scope note: the typed alzheimer-s-disease identity already carries an insomnia edge; this batch authors no dementia-insomnia edge to avoid the parallel-pathway pattern, and generic-dementia consolidation is recorded as a governance decision.

Anxiety is measured as a neuropsychiatric symptom (NPI); whether any patient's presentation meets independent anxiety-disorder criteria is an individual clinician determination this mapping cannot make.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The Alzheimer's NPS meta-analysis (48 studies) found anxiety the fourth most prevalent neuropsychiatric symptom in AD at 39% (95% CI 32-46%) (Zhao 2016); the mild-AD cross-sectional study found anxiety in 65% of mild-AD patients, independently associated with worse basic and instrumental daily functioning (Spalletta 2010).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: anxiety here is mostly measured as a neuropsychiatric SYMPTOM of the dementing process rather than as an independent disorder diagnosis; emotional or behavioral symptoms are partly defining features of dementia (identity-restatement guard); caregiver-population prevalence studies do not transfer to the patient; and no directional cohort separates dementia-driven anxiety from awareness-of-deficit reactive anxiety.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized network-disintegration pathway: progressive loss of limbic and prefrontal regulatory circuitry reduces top-down inhibition of the fear/anxiety networks, so threat appraisal becomes dysregulated as neurodegeneration advances, presenting clinically as NPI-scored anxiety. Whether any patient's anxiety reflects this mechanism rather than preserved-insight distress is individual and unquantified.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Anxiety prevalence is AD-population NPI measurement, not independent-disorder incidence; behavioral and psychiatric symptoms are partly defining features of dementia, so symptom-to-disorder attribution is a clinical judgment; delirium, medications, and thyroid disease must be excluded; caregiver studies do not transfer to patients.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documented dementia diagnosis with anxiety features predating or independent of delirium; DSM-5-TR delirium exclusion; medication and thyroid review; a qualified clinician's assessment of whether the anxiety meets independent disorder criteria rather than dementia-behavior description
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Anticholinergic, dopaminergic, or corticosteroid medication effects

evidenceGaps: Documented dementia diagnosis with anxiety features predating or independent of delirium; DSM-5-TR delirium exclusion; medication and thyroid review; a qualified clinician's assessment of whether the anxiety meets independent disorder criteria rather than dementia-behavior description
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: in-dementia anxiety is highly prevalent and mechanistically plausible, but it is measured as a neuropsychiatric symptom of the disease and any independent disorder diagnosis requires individual clinician determination; no causal claim is forced.

sourceReferences.citation: Zhao QF, Tan L, Wang HF, Jiang T, Tan MS, Tan L, Xu W, Li JQ, Wang J, Lai TJ, Yu JT. The prevalence of neuropsychiatric symptoms in Alzheimer's disease: Systematic review and meta-analysis. J Affect Disord. 2016 Jan 15;190:264-271. PMID 26540080.
sourceReferences.note: Meta-analysis of 48 studies: anxiety is the fourth most prevalent neuropsychiatric symptom in Alzheimer's disease at 39% (95% CI 32-46%); sleep disorder 39%, depression 42%.

sourceReferences.citation: Spalletta G, Girardi P, Caltagirone C, Orfei MD. Neuropsychiatric symptoms and IADL in mild Alzheimer's disease: anxiety as a clinical marker. J Alzheimers Dis. 2010;21(1):45-54. PMID 20308732.
sourceReferences.note: Cross-sectional study: anxiety was present in 65% of mild-AD patients and independently associated with worse basic and instrumental daily functioning.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The interRAI national cohort (n=7775 community-dwelling people with dementia) found 1-year UI prevalence of 50.1% and an adjusted 5-year incident-UI hazard ratio of 1.4 versus non-dementia controls (Burholt 2024); the global meta-analysis pooled UI prevalence in dementia at 39.7% (95% CI 23.9-58.1%), higher in clinic/hospital than community settings (Moradi Sarcheshmeh 2026).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the CNS small vessel disease review documents that the same small-vessel pathology independently causes both dementia and urinary incontinence (shared-cause confound); the meta-analysis's 4%-88% prevalence span reflects setting and assessment-method heterogeneity; no directional cohort separates neurogenic detrusor overactivity from mobility, communication, or toileting-access components of incontinence in dementia.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized frontal-micturition-disinhibition pathway: progressive frontal and white-matter neurodegeneration disrupts the prefrontal and pontine micturition-control networks that normally inhibit voiding reflexes; reduced inhibition plus impaired mobility, recognition of need, and communication presents clinically as urge incontinence. How much of any patient's UI is neurogenic versus functional is individual and unquantified.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Cohort prevalence does not establish etiology; CSVD independently causes both conditions; functional (mobility, access, communication) incontinence components are indistinguishable from neurogenic components in dementia populations; Parkinson's disease, prostate disease, impaction, and diuretics dominate individual risk in the same cohorts; institutional-care measurement settings inflate prevalence.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Documented dementia with incontinence chronology; urologic workup excluding outlet obstruction, prostate disease in men, atrophic changes in women, and fecal impaction; medication review (diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics); mobility and toileting-access assessment
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Benign prostatic hyperplasia and bladder outlet obstruction (men)
CNS small vessel disease as an independent shared cause of both dementia and incontinence
Parkinson's disease comorbidity (OR 3.0 in the same cohort)

evidenceGaps: Documented dementia with incontinence chronology; urologic workup excluding outlet obstruction, prostate disease in men, atrophic changes in women, and fecal impaction; medication review (diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics); mobility and toileting-access assessment
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: prevalence is large-cohort quantified, but the shared small-vessel-cause confound is documented in the pathway literature and the functional component of incontinence in dementia cannot be separated at the mapping level; no causal claim is forced.

sourceReferences.citation: Burholt V, Cheung G, Awatere SA, Daltrey JF. Incidence, Prevalence, and Risk for Urinary Incontinence for People with Dementia in the Community in Aotearoa New Zealand: An interRAI Study. J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2024 Nov;25(11):105285. PMID 39326857.
sourceReferences.note: National retrospective cohort (n=7775): 1-year UI prevalence 50.1% among community-dwelling people with dementia; 5-year incident UI 30.2 per 100 person-years versus 24.5 in non-dementia controls; adjusted HR 1.4 for dementia.
